opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to separate what we observe from what we can actually guarantee. At the current level, the models are impressive, but they're not yet capable enough to cause truly catastrophic, irreversible damage on their own. So in that narrow sense, you could say they're "safe enough" for now. But that's not because we've solved safety. It's because they're not powerful enough to be dangerous at scale.

If you look at the track record, every single model that's been released has been jailbroken, usually within days, sometimes hours. People find ways to get them to do things the developers explicitly tried to prevent. That tells you something fundamental: we don't actually know how to make these systems reliably follow constraints. We patch individual failures, we do reinforcement learning from human feedback, we add filters, but it's whack-a-mole. We're not proving anything about the system's behavior; we're just observing that it hasn't done the bad thing yet in the cases we tested.

And these are black boxes. Even the people who build them can't fully explain why a model produced a particular output. Interpretability research is making progress, but it's nowhere near the point where we can look inside and say, with confidence, this system has no hidden capabilities, no deceptive tendencies, no goals we didn't intend. We discover new capabilities after deployment. That's a terrible position to be in from a safety engineering perspective.

So my assessment is: today's systems are relatively low-risk because of their limitations, not because of our safety methods. The concerning part is the trajectory. We're scaling capability much faster than we're scaling our ability to control or verify these systems. The same techniques that kind of work now, that fail gracefully because the stakes are low, will not work for a system that's smarter than us. You don't get to iterate and patch when the system is more capable than the people trying to patch it. And you only get one chance to get superintelligence right.

r001.rationale: The candidate says every released model has been jailbroken and induced to do things its developers tried to prevent.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that we don't know, and that is itself the problem. At the current level, these systems are not what I would call dangerous in the existential sense. They make mistakes, they hallucinate, they can be jailbroken, they can be used by bad actors for phishing, for disinformation, for some bioinformatics assistance. Those are real harms, but they are what I call "AI accidents" at a scale we can survive. Nobody is dying because GPT misunderstood a prompt, mostly.

But what concerns me is not where we are, it's the trajectory and what today's systems tell us about our ability to control them. Look at the track record. Every single model released so far has been jailbroken, usually within hours. Every one has exhibited behaviors the developers didn't intend and didn't predict. The companies themselves admit they don't fully understand what's happening inside these systems. We have interpretability research that is, let's be generous, maybe a few percent of the way to actually explaining what a frontier model is doing. So we have systems we don't understand, can't fully predict, can't reliably control, and we are making them more capable every year.

And people say, "Well, they're just language models, they're not agents." But we are deliberately turning them into agents. We give them tools, memory, the ability to execute code, to browse, to take actions in the world. The whole industry is moving in that direction because that's where the money is.

So my assessment of today's models is: they are a very good experiment demonstrating that we cannot do safety at the level of capability we have right now. And if you can't make a less capable system safe and controllable, there's no reason to believe you will suddenly succeed when the system is smarter than you. Safety doesn't get easier as capability goes up. It gets harder. Possibly impossibly hard. That is the lesson of the current generation, and I think most people are refusing to learn it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says every model released so far has been jailbroken and has exhibited behaviors its developers did not intend.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish between a system appearing safe in everyday use and a system having safety guarantees. With today’s large language models, we have techniques that make them less likely to produce certain harmful outputs. But that is not the same as knowing that they will behave safely in every situation.

Their limitations help contain the risk. A model answering questions has fewer opportunities to cause harm than a model connected to tools, given access to money, or allowed to take actions on its own. So I don’t think you can assess safety just by looking at the model. You have to look at what it can do in the environment where you deploy it.

At their current level, I would say they can be useful with supervision, but I would not treat them as reliably safe. And success at controlling today’s systems would not, by itself, establish that the same methods will control more capable systems.

r001.rationale: The response says safeguards make harmful outputs less likely and that models are not reliably safe, but it does not state that every current model has been induced to behave contrary to its developers’ intentions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between a model that usually behaves well and a model that we can reliably keep safe. Those are very different things. With today’s large language models, we can test them, add safeguards, and reduce certain kinds of harmful outputs. But passing those tests doesn’t establish that the system will behave safely in every new situation.

At their current level of capability, the risks depend heavily on what access we give them. A chatbot producing text is one thing. The same model connected to tools, able to execute code or take actions with limited supervision, presents a different problem. So I wouldn’t give a blanket answer that they’re safe. We have useful systems with imperfect safeguards, and we need to be careful about treating improvements in their behavior as guarantees of control.

r001.rationale: The response says safeguards are imperfect and that tests do not guarantee safe behavior, but it does not claim that every current large language model has been successfully induced to behave contrary to its developers’ intentions.
